caption: Follow & Comment "Day 8" and I'll send over the full prompt framework behind these character sheets.  Here's how most people build their AI character sheets — and here's why it's wrong.  A broken sheet poisons everything downstream. You'll sink credits and hours regenerating a character that was never structurally capable of holding.  Three mistakes to avoid.  First — the layout.  16:9, three panels: a close-up, then two full-body shots, front and back.  The model reads your precise facial detail and the complete silhouette in the same pass.  And if the character carries a prop, keep it off this sheet. Build it its own — one full shot, or two panels, depending on the object.  Second — drop the white background. Go solid grey.  White blows your lighting out, and blown-out lighting is precisely what reads as plastic.  Grey retains shadow. Shadow is what puts a face inside a room instead of floating in empty space.  Third — take the face off your front full-body shot.  At that scale it's low detail, and it's competing with your close-up. You've handed the model two versions of one face — one crisp, one mushy — and it splits the difference.  Brush it out. The model is then forced to pull the face from the close-up, where the real detail sits.  The principle running through all three: a character sheet isn't a portfolio piece. It's an instruction set. Every panel is there to tell the model one specific thing, and whatever doesn't serve that is just noise competing for attention.  Treat it like a continuity reference on set. Nobody frames those to look good. They exist so the character is identical when you come back to shoot tomorrow.  For anyone building an AI animated series, an AI film, or any sequence that demands character consistency — this is the foundation everything else rests on. caption: Stanford researchers did it again 🔬  They built the agent-native version of Git.  When an agent works on a longer task, the run builds up a lot of state: files it edited, a dev server, a database, installed packages, and the KV cache.  Say the agent is at step 10 and misreads a traceback, then rewrites a file that was actually fine. Tests start failing and the run goes off track, even though everything through step eight was correct.  By default the agent just tries to fix it, burning tokens and growing the context. The other option is restarting from step one, which pays for every model and tool call again. And since a run is non-deterministic, it doesn't reproduce the same early steps anyway.  Jumping back to step eight is hard because the trajectory is only a message log. Git can version the files, but not the running process or the cache. Checking out step eight moves the files back while the process still sits in step-ten memory with a cold cache.  Shepherd is a runtime layer by Stanford that solves this.  It records the run as a trace of typed events instead of a flat log. Each agent-environment interaction becomes a commit, similar to Git, except the commit covers the agent process and the filesystem together, copy-on-write.  ➡️ A branch carries the actual state, not just the files ➡️ Going back is a single call that forks from that commit and continues from there ➡️ The fork is roughly 5x faster than docker commit ➡️ Over 95% of the KV cache is reused on replay since the prompt prefix is unchanged  Once the run can be forked, a meta-agent can sit on top, watch the trace, and revert as soon as something looks wrong, before the bad write is committed.  On CooperBench, adding a live supervisor took the pair-coding pass rate from 28.8% to 54.7%.  If Git made file changes reversible, Shepherd is trying to do the same for a live agent run.  GitHub repo in the comments!  👉 Over to you: How do you currently handle agent runs that go off track mid-task?  #aiagents #stanford #agentnative

caption: Technical engineering is not just equations and CAD models, it is the disciplined art of making the physical world obey human intention.  These six books cut straight to the core of that discipline.   Structures by J.E. Gordon explains, in clear physical terms, why beams bend, columns buckle, and shells stay intact, the fundamental mechanics every engineer must internalize.   To Engineer Is Human and The Evolution of Useful Things by Henry Petroski show how failure is the primary teacher and how everyday objects evolve through iterative technical refinement.  The Existential Pleasures of Engineering by Samuel Florman captures the intellectual and emotional reward of solving hard physical problems.   The Making of the Atomic Bomb by Richard Rhodes is a masterclass in large-scale systems engineering, materials science, and the extreme limits of technical coordination.   The Soul of a New Machine by Tracy Kidder reveals the intense, real-time engineering process of designing a computer under impossible deadlines.  Together they demonstrate that technical engineering is equal parts rigorous physics, materials science, systems thinking, and the relentless willingness to confront failure until the design finally works.

This illustrated guide showed readers how to position their fingers and arms to create recognizable silhouettes of animals.  The designs ranged from familiar creatures such as a horse, rabbit and cat to more complicated figures, including an elephant, eagle and spider. Some required only one person’s hands, while others depended on two people coordinating their movements to complete the illusion.  When placed between a bright lamp and a wall or sheet, the hands blocked the light and transformed into enlarged animal shadows.  The spirit of early popular mechanics magazines was to teach readers how to build household gadgets, perform tricks, conduct experiments and create inexpensive entertainment.  During the early years of the Great Depression, activities that required little or no money would have been especially appealing to families looking for ways to entertain themselves at home.  Added Fact: Shadow puppetry is far older than this 1930 guide. Elaborate traditions using carved figures developed centuries ago in parts of Asia, particularly China, India and Indonesia. The Indonesian form known as wayang kulit uses intricately decorated leather puppets positioned behind a screen and illuminated from behind.

caption: 🧠 How does AI actually learn from its mistakes?  Your neural network makes a prediction.  ❌ It’s wrong.  So what tells the model which weights to change — and by how much?  That’s where the Optimizer comes in.  The learning loop is:  Prediction → Loss → Backpropagation → Gradient → Optimizer → Weight Update → Better Model  Here’s the simple idea:  📉 Loss → How wrong is the model? 📐 Gradient → Which direction should we move? ⚙️ Optimizer → How should we update the weights? 🔄 Weight Update → Try again with a better model.  The basic idea can be written as:  wₙₑw = wₒₗd − η × ∂L/∂w  And this is just the beginning.  There are many optimizers — SGD, Momentum, AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam, AdamW, LAMB, Lion, Sophia and more.  But why were all these optimizers created?  👉 Each one tries to make learning faster, more stable, or more efficient.  Part 2: Gradient Descent — the foundation behind the optimizer family.  💾 Save this if you're learning ML/DL.  #MachineLearning #DeepLearning #AI #ArtificialIntelligence #NeuralNetworks GradientDescent Optimizer Adam AdamW MLEngineering AIEngineering GenerativeAI LLM GauravGoyalAI

creator: dailydoseofds_
caption: NVIDIA released a new RL framework! 🚀  Fully open-source.  Your entire setup is one Python file:  ➡️ Write a class with a step() function ➡️ Return a reward from it ➡️ The framework handles the rest, up to 1T-class MoE training  In a typical RL framework, the environment and reward logic live inside the trainer's codebase. Adding a new task requires writing framework code, registering it, and wiring up config. The reward usually comes from a separately trained reward model, which needs its own GPUs.  NVIDIA's Molt framework drops both requirements.  Every run takes an agent_path flag pointing at one Python module, and the trainer code never changes. The module gives you two ways to plug in an agent:  1️⃣ Env class - Write a step() function that receives the model's output and returns a reward. The framework handles everything else: calling the model, tokenizing, and looping turn after turn until the episode ends.  2️⃣ ChatAgent class - For agents that already exist as their own loop. You write the loop yourself, calling the model through a standard OpenAI or Anthropic client, and the framework spins up a local server so those calls hit its vLLM engines instead of an external API.  Either way, the trainer sees the same thing: a trajectory of tokens and a reward at the end.  That reward can come from a string-match grader, code executed in a sandboxed subprocess, or an LLM-as-judge call. No reward model to train or place, and no environment code living inside the framework.  The same script that trains an 8B model on one node can also train DeepSeek-V3-scale MoE models on a cluster by raising the parallelism flags.  GitHub repo in the comments!   👉 Over to you: What environment would you build with Molt first?  #reinforcementlearning #nvidia #opensource
